# Rule reference

Every control of a profile and the checks that decide it. A control passes only when every
check applicable to it passes; checks that cannot decide report `MANUAL` or `ERROR`, never
`PASS` (see [ADR 0006](adr/0006-rule-format-evaluation-results.md)). Control IDs come from the
standard; titles and descriptions are hostlint's own. Parameters can be made stricter in
[hostlint.yaml](configuration.md).

### Checks

#### `accounts.lockout-threshold`

Accounts lock after repeated login failures (로그인에 여러 번 실패하면 계정이 잠김) — severity high, evaluates an expression.

Checks that the login and (when an SSH server is present) sshd PAM stacks lock an account after at most `max_failures` failed attempts, with pam_faillock or pam_tally2. pam_faillock only locks with an authfail line plus a preauth or authsucc line, and sshd only uses PAM with UsePAM yes.

**Why.** Without a lockout, an attacker can try passwords against an account indefinitely.

**Fix.** Enable pam_faillock (authselect enable-feature with-faillock, or preauth, authfail and account lines on Debian), set `deny = 10` or less in /etc/security/faillock.conf, and keep `UsePAM yes` in sshd_config.

**Parameters.**

- `max_failures` (int, default `10`, lower is stricter): Failed attempts before an account locks

#### `accounts.passwd-no-hashes`

No password hashes or empty passwords in /etc/passwd (/etc/passwd에 비밀번호 해시나 빈 비밀번호 없음) — severity high, lists what violates it.

Lists accounts whose /etc/passwd password field holds a hash or is empty instead of pointing to /etc/shadow ("x").

**Why.** /etc/passwd is readable by every user, so a hash there can be cracked offline, and an empty field means no password at all.

**Fix.** Run `pwconv` to move passwords to /etc/shadow, and lock or set passwords for empty ones.

#### `accounts.password-complexity`

Passwords mix letters, digits and special characters (비밀번호에 영문자·숫자·특수문자를 섞어 씀) — severity high, evaluates an expression.

Checks that password quality, not in warning-only mode, requires at least one digit, one special character and one letter (upper or lower case): dcredit, ocredit and ucredit or lcredit set to -1 or less, or minclass 4 (every character class), or minclass 3 together with dcredit and ocredit (a letter is then the third class).

**Why.** Passwords drawn from one character class are far easier to guess.

**Fix.** Set `dcredit = -1`, `ocredit = -1`, `ucredit = -1` and `lcredit = -1` (or `minclass = 4`, or `minclass = 3` with `dcredit = -1` and `ocredit = -1`) in /etc/security/pwquality.conf.

#### `accounts.password-hash-method`

New passwords use a strong hash (새 비밀번호가 강한 해시를 씀) — severity medium, evaluates an expression.

Checks that new passwords get a SHA-2, yescrypt or bcrypt hash: the hashing option of pam_unix in the passwd stack, which overrides login.defs for passwd, and ENCRYPT_METHOD in /etc/login.defs, used by the other shadow-utils tools. ENCRYPT_METHOD YESCRYPT only counts where shadow-utils is built with yescrypt (Debian 12, Ubuntu 24.04, RHEL 10 and their successors); elsewhere, such as RHEL 9 and Ubuntu 22.04, it falls back to DES.

**Why.** Passwords hashed with DES or MD5 crypt can be cracked quickly once the hash leaks.

**Fix.** Set `ENCRYPT_METHOD SHA512` in /etc/login.defs, use sha512 or yescrypt on the pam_unix password line, then have users change their passwords.

#### `accounts.password-hash-strength`

Stored passwords use a strong hash (저장된 비밀번호가 강한 해시를 씀) — severity medium, lists what violates it.

Lists accounts whose /etc/shadow hash uses DES, MD5 or an unrecognized scheme. Without /etc/shadow there is nothing to check, so the check cannot pass.

**Why.** Changing ENCRYPT_METHOD only affects new passwords; old weak hashes stay crackable.

**Fix.** Have the listed users change their passwords (passwd -e user forces it at next login).

#### `accounts.password-history`

Recent passwords cannot be reused (최근 비밀번호를 다시 쓸 수 없음) — severity medium, evaluates an expression.

Checks that the passwd service rejects any of the last `remember` passwords, also when root sets the password: pam_pwhistory with enforce_for_root, whose rejection keeps pam_unix from storing the password. pam_unix's remember option does not count, since pam_unix skips the check when root changes a password.

**Why.** Reusing old passwords brings back credentials that may already be known.

**Fix.** Enable pam_pwhistory before pam_unix in the password stack and set `remember = 4` (or more) and `enforce_for_root` in /etc/security/pwhistory.conf or on the module line.

**Parameters.**

- `remember` (int, default `4`, higher is stricter): Number of previous passwords remembered

#### `accounts.password-max-age`

Passwords expire (비밀번호가 만료됨) — severity medium, compares one setting.

Checks PASS_MAX_DAYS in /etc/login.defs, the maximum password age given to new accounts. Without it, shadow-utils uses -1, which means passwords never expire.

**Why.** A password that never changes stays useful to whoever obtained it.

**Fix.** Set `PASS_MAX_DAYS 90` (or less) in /etc/login.defs; apply it to existing accounts with chage.

**Parameters.**

- `max_days` (int, default `90`, lower is stricter): Maximum password age in days

#### `accounts.password-max-age-existing`

Existing accounts have expiring passwords (기존 계정의 비밀번호가 만료됨) — severity medium, lists what violates it.

Lists accounts with a password whose own maximum age in /etc/shadow is empty, 0 or more than `max_days`. The login.defs value only applies to accounts created after it was set, so an existing account (root keeps 99999 on many systems) can still never expire.

**Why.** A password that never changes stays useful to whoever obtained it.

**Fix.** Run `chage -M 90 account` for each listed account, and set `PASS_MAX_DAYS 90` in /etc/login.defs for new ones.

**Parameters.**

- `max_days` (int, default `90`, lower is stricter): Maximum password age in days

#### `accounts.password-min-age`

Passwords cannot be changed back at once (비밀번호를 바로 되돌려 바꿀 수 없음) — severity low, compares one setting.

Checks PASS_MIN_DAYS in /etc/login.defs, the minimum days between password changes.

**Why.** Without a minimum age, a user can cycle through passwords in minutes to get back to the old one and defeat the password history.

**Fix.** Set `PASS_MIN_DAYS 1` (or more) in /etc/login.defs.

**Parameters.**

- `min_days` (int, default `1`, higher is stricter): Minimum password age in days

#### `accounts.password-min-length`

Passwords have a minimum length (비밀번호에 최소 길이가 있음) — severity high, evaluates an expression.

Checks that the passwd service's PAM stack enforces password quality (pam_pwquality or pam_cracklib, not in warning-only mode) with a minimum length of at least `min_length` characters. Positive credits let a password be shorter by up to their sum, so they count against minlen.

**Why.** Short passwords fall quickly to guessing and offline cracking.

**Fix.** Enable pam_pwquality in the password stack (authselect, pam-auth-update), set `minlen = 8` or more in /etc/security/pwquality.conf, and do not set enforcing = 0 or positive credits.

**Parameters.**

- `min_length` (int, default `8`, higher is stricter): Minimum password length

#### `accounts.password-quality-root`

Password quality also applies to root (비밀번호 품질 검사가 root에도 적용됨) — severity medium, evaluates an expression.

Checks that the password-quality module, not in warning-only mode, has enforce_for_root, so root cannot set a weak password after the warning.

**Why.** Without enforce_for_root, quality rules only warn when root changes a password.

**Fix.** Add `enforce_for_root` to /etc/security/pwquality.conf. On CentOS/RHEL 7 (libpwquality 1.2) that file has no such setting: add it as an argument of the pam_pwquality line in /etc/pam.d/system-auth and password-auth instead.

#### `accounts.review-admin-groups`

Review members of administrative groups (관리자 그룹 구성원 검토) — severity medium, a review (`MANUAL`).

Lists the members of the root (GID 0), wheel, sudo and admin groups: the accounts whose primary group it is (/etc/passwd), which pam_wheel and sudo count as members too, and the supplementary members listed in /etc/group.

**Why.** Every member of these groups can gain or already has administrative power.

**Fix.** Remove accounts that do not need administrative rights (gpasswd -d user group).

#### `accounts.review-empty-groups`

Review groups without accounts (계정이 속하지 않은 그룹 검토) — severity low, a review (`MANUAL`).

Lists groups that have no members and are no account's primary group.

**Why.** Unused groups can still own files and be reused by a new account by mistake.

**Fix.** Remove groups that are not needed (groupdel), after checking which files they own.

#### `accounts.review-login-accounts`

Review accounts that can log in (로그인할 수 있는 계정 검토) — severity low, a review (`MANUAL`).

Lists every account with a login shell, for a reviewer to confirm each is still needed.

**Why.** Accounts left behind by departed users or old services are easy targets.

**Fix.** Remove accounts that are no longer needed (userdel). An account that must stay but should not log in gets a nologin shell and a locked password (usermod -L -s /usr/sbin/nologin).

#### `accounts.session-timeout-set`

Idle shells time out (유휴 셸이 자동으로 끝남) — severity low, compares one setting.

Checks that the system-wide startup files (/etc/environment, /etc/profile and the files it reads, such as /etc/profile.d) leave TMOUT set to a positive number of seconds, so that it applies to every user's login shell: a value set only in root's own files does not count, assignments inside if or case blocks do not count, and a later unset removes it.

**Why.** An unattended logged-in terminal can be used by anyone who reaches it.

**Fix.** Add `TMOUT=600` and `readonly TMOUT` and `export TMOUT` to a file in /etc/profile.d.

#### `accounts.session-timeout-value`

The idle timeout is short enough (유휴 시간 제한이 충분히 짧음) — severity low, lists what violates it.

Lists TMOUT assignments that are empty, zero or longer than `max_seconds`, and unset TMOUT commands, including those inside if or case blocks, which can apply to some sessions.

**Why.** A long or disabled timeout leaves idle sessions open.

**Fix.** Set `TMOUT=600` (or less) and remove larger assignments and unset commands.

**Parameters.**

- `max_seconds` (int, default `600`, lower is stricter): Longest acceptable idle timeout in seconds

#### `accounts.shadow-file`

Password hashes are kept in /etc/shadow (비밀번호 해시는 /etc/shadow에 보관) — severity high, evaluates an expression.

Checks that /etc/shadow exists, so hashes are kept out of the world-readable /etc/passwd.

**Why.** Without /etc/shadow, password hashes have to live in /etc/passwd where anyone can read them.

**Fix.** Run `pwconv` (and `grpconv` for groups).

#### `accounts.su-wheel-only`

Only members of the wheel group can use su (wheel 그룹 구성원만 su를 쓸 수 있음) — severity high, compares one setting.

Checks that the su PAM stack has a pam_wheel line that denies users outside the wheel group (or the group given with group=), or that su itself is restricted by its permissions (owned by root, group wheel, sudo, admin or adm, setuid, not executable by others). A line with trust or deny, a control that does not deny (optional, sufficient), or a sufficient rule earlier in the stack does not restrict su.

**Why.** Without the restriction, any user who learns the root password can become root with su.

**Fix.** Add `auth required pam_wheel.so use_uid` to /etc/pam.d/su, before the common-auth or system-auth include, and add administrators to the wheel group. Or restrict the program to an administrators' group (`chgrp wheel /usr/bin/su && chmod 4750 /usr/bin/su`; on Debian and Ubuntu use the group sudo and `dpkg-statoverride`, so that package updates keep it).

#### `accounts.system-account-shells`

System accounts cannot log in (시스템 계정은 로그인할 수 없음) — severity low, lists what violates it.

Lists system accounts (UID 1 to `system_uid_max`, and the overflow accounts such as nobody, UID 65534 or 4294967294) that have a login shell instead of nologin or false.

**Why.** A service account with a shell gives an attacker who reaches it an interactive foothold.

**Fix.** Set the shell to /usr/sbin/nologin (usermod -s /usr/sbin/nologin account).

**Parameters.**

- `system_uid_max` (int, default `999`, higher is stricter): Highest UID of system accounts

#### `accounts.uid0-only-root`

Only root has UID 0 (UID 0은 root만 가짐) — severity high, lists what violates it.

Lists accounts other than root whose UID is 0.

**Why.** Every UID 0 account has full root privileges, under a name that may escape notice.

**Fix.** Give the account another UID (usermod -u) or remove it.

#### `accounts.unique-uids`

Every account has its own UID (계정마다 UID가 다름) — severity medium, lists what violates it.

Lists accounts that share a UID with another account.

**Why.** Accounts sharing a UID are the same user to the kernel, so access and audit trails cannot tell them apart.

**Fix.** Give each account a unique UID (usermod -u) and fix the ownership of its files.

#### `env.path-current-dir`

PATH does not search the current directory first (PATH에서 현재 디렉터리를 먼저 찾지 않음) — severity high, lists what violates it.

Lists PATH assignments in the system-wide and root's startup files that put the current directory (".", or an empty entry) anywhere but last.

**Why.** With the current directory early in PATH, a program named like a system command in the directory you are in runs instead of it, as you.

**Fix.** Remove "." and empty entries from PATH, or move them to the end.

#### `env.umask-login-defs`

The default umask keeps new files unwritable by group and others (기본 umask가 그룹·기타 사용자의 쓰기를 막음 (login.defs)) — severity medium, compares one setting.

Checks that UMASK in /etc/login.defs removes write permission for group and others (022 or stricter). shadow-utils and pam_umask use it for new sessions and home directories.

**Why.** A permissive umask makes new files writable by other users.

**Fix.** Set `UMASK 022` (or `027`) in /etc/login.defs.

#### `env.umask-startup-files`

Startup files do not set a permissive umask (시작 파일이 느슨한 umask를 설정하지 않음) — severity medium, lists what violates it.

Lists umask commands in the system-wide and root's startup files that leave write permission for group or others, including those inside if or case blocks, and symbolic ones to review.

**Why.** A permissive umask in a startup file overrides the system default for every session.

**Fix.** Use `umask 022` (or stricter) and remove permissive or symbolic umask commands.

#### `files.at-spool`

Queued at jobs are private (at 작업 큐는 본인만 접근할 수 있음) — severity high, reads file metadata.

Checks that the queued jobs and sequence file of at (/var/spool/at on the RHEL family, /var/spool/cron/atjobs on Debian and Ubuntu) can be read, written and run by their owner only (mode 0700 or stricter).

**Why.** A job other users can change runs their commands as the job's owner.

**Fix.** Run `chmod 700` on each listed job.

#### `files.cron-commands`

Only root and a group can run crontab and at (crontab·at 명령은 일반 사용자 실행 금지) — severity high, reads file metadata.

Checks that /usr/bin/crontab and /usr/bin/at are owned by root and cannot be run by other users (no execute permission for others; mode 6750 or stricter).

**Why.** Scheduled jobs keep running after a user is gone; letting every user schedule them widens what an intruder can persist.

**Fix.** Run `chmod o-x /usr/bin/crontab /usr/bin/at`, and let users who need them in through the file's group.

#### `files.cron-files`

cron and at configuration is owned by root and not readable by others (cron·at 설정 파일은 root 소유, 다른 사용자 읽기 금지) — severity high, reads file metadata.

Checks that /etc/crontab, /etc/cron.d/*, and the cron and at allow and deny files are owned by root with mode 0640 or stricter.

**Why.** These files decide what runs as root on a schedule and who may schedule jobs.

**Fix.** Run `chown root` and `chmod 640` on each listed file.

#### `files.cron-root-spool`

Root's crontab is root's and private (root의 crontab은 root 소유이며 root만 읽고 쓸 수 있음) — severity high, reads file metadata.

Checks that root's crontab (/var/spool/cron/crontabs/root on Debian and Ubuntu, /var/spool/cron/root on the RHEL family) is owned by root and can be read and written by root only (mode 0600 or stricter).

**Why.** Whoever can change root's crontab runs commands as root.

**Fix.** Run `chown root` and `chmod 600` on the listed crontab.

#### `files.cron-scripts`

Scheduled script directories are owned by root and not writable by others (cron 스크립트 디렉터리는 root 소유, 다른 사용자 쓰기 금지) — severity high, reads file metadata.

Checks that the scripts in /etc/cron.hourly, /etc/cron.daily, /etc/cron.weekly and /etc/cron.monthly are owned by root and writable by no one else (mode 0755 or stricter).

**Why.** These scripts run as root on a schedule; whoever can change one gets root at the next run.

**Fix.** Run `chown root` and `chmod go-w` on each listed script.

#### `files.cron-spool`

Users' crontabs are private (사용자 crontab은 본인만 읽고 쓸 수 있음) — severity high, reads file metadata.

Checks that the crontab files in /var/spool/cron/crontabs (Debian and Ubuntu) can be read and written by their owner only (mode 0600 or stricter). Root's crontab, which must also belong to root, is files.cron-root-spool. Users' crontabs in /var/spool/cron on the RHEL family are files.cron-spool-rhel.

**Why.** A crontab other users can change runs commands as its owner, root's as root.

**Fix.** Run `chmod 600` on each listed crontab.

#### `files.cron-spool-rhel`

Users' crontabs on the RHEL family are private (RHEL 계열의 사용자 crontab은 본인만 읽고 쓸 수 있음) — severity high, reads file metadata.

Checks that the crontab files in /var/spool/cron (RHEL family) can be read and written by their owner only (mode 0600 or stricter). Debian and Ubuntu keep them in /var/spool/cron/crontabs, which is files.cron-spool. Root's crontab must also belong to root (files.cron-root-spool).

**Why.** A crontab other users can change runs commands as its owner, root's as root.

**Fix.** Run `chmod 600` on each listed crontab.

#### `files.dev-regular-files`

No regular files in /dev (/dev에 일반 파일 없음) — severity high, lists what violates it.

Lists regular files under /dev (outside /dev/shm and /dev/mqueue), where only devices and directories belong.

**Why.** /dev is rarely looked at, which makes it a place to hide files; a regular file there holds no device.

**Fix.** Check what each listed file is and remove the ones that do not belong.

#### `files.hosts-lpd-perms`

/etc/hosts.lpd is owned by root and private, if it exists (/etc/hosts.lpd는 있으면 root 소유, 비공개) — severity low, reads file metadata.

Checks that /etc/hosts.lpd, if present, is owned by root with mode 0600 or stricter.

**Why.** The file lists hosts allowed to print; whoever can change it can open the print service to others.

**Fix.** Remove /etc/hosts.lpd if printing from other hosts is not needed; otherwise `chown root` and `chmod 600` it.

#### `files.hosts-perms`

/etc/hosts is owned by root and not writable by others (/etc/hosts는 root 소유, 다른 사용자 쓰기 금지) — severity high, reads file metadata.

Checks that /etc/hosts is owned by root with mode 0644 or stricter.

**Why.** Whoever can write /etc/hosts can redirect host names to their own addresses.

**Fix.** Run `chown root /etc/hosts` and `chmod 644 /etc/hosts`.

#### `files.inetd-conf-perms`

inetd and xinetd configuration is owned by root and private (inetd·xinetd 설정은 root 소유, 비공개) — severity high, reads file metadata.

Checks that /etc/inetd.conf, /etc/xinetd.conf and the files in /etc/xinetd.d are owned by root with mode 0600 or stricter. Not applicable when none exists.

**Why.** The super-server starts the programs these files name, as the users they name.

**Fix.** Run `chown root` and `chmod 600` on each file.

#### `files.log-world-writable`

Log files cannot be changed by every user (로그 파일을 모든 사용자가 수정할 수 없음) — severity medium, lists what violates it.

Lists files and directories under /var/log that every user can write (directories without the sticky bit). Who owns them is for files.review-log-files.

**Why.** Whoever can change a log can remove the trace of what they did.

**Fix.** Remove write permission for others (`chmod o-w`), or set the sticky bit on a shared directory (`chmod +t`).

#### `files.passwd-perms`

/etc/passwd is owned by root and not writable by others (/etc/passwd는 root 소유, 다른 사용자 쓰기 금지) — severity high, reads file metadata.

Checks that /etc/passwd is owned by root with mode 0644 or stricter.

**Why.** Anyone who can write /etc/passwd can add an account with UID 0.

**Fix.** Run `chown root /etc/passwd` and `chmod 644 /etc/passwd`.

#### `files.review-hidden-files`

Review hidden files and directories (숨김 파일·디렉터리 검토) — severity low, a review (`MANUAL`).

Hidden files (names starting with ".") hold user settings, and also what someone wants out of a listing.

**Why.** Hidden files and directories are where unexpected content goes unnoticed.

**Fix.** Remove the ones that do not belong.

#### `files.review-log-files`

Review who owns the log files (로그 파일 소유자 검토) — severity medium, a review (`MANUAL`).

Lists the files and directories under /var/log that root does not own.

**Why.** A log owned by a login account can be rewritten by whoever uses it; one owned by the logging service is expected.

**Fix.** Run `chown root` on logs that no service writes as another account.

#### `files.review-setid`

Review the set-ID programs (SUID·SGID 파일 검토) — severity medium, a review (`MANUAL`).

Lists every file with the set-user-ID or set-group-ID bit on local filesystems.

**Why.** Each set-ID program runs with its owner's or group's rights; the ones nobody needs only add risk.

**Fix.** Remove the set-ID bits (`chmod u-s,g-s`) from programs your users do not need, or limit who can run them.

#### `files.rhosts`

.rhosts and hosts.equiv files are owned correctly and private (.rhosts·hosts.equiv는 root 소유, 비공개) — severity high, reads file metadata.

Checks that /etc/hosts.equiv and the .rhosts files of root and home directories under /home are owned by root and private (mode 0600 or stricter). Such files should not exist unless the r-services are needed.

**Why.** These files let hosts and users log in through rlogin and rsh without a password.

**Fix.** Remove the files; if the r-services are really needed, `chmod 600` them and never use "+" entries.

#### `files.services-perms`

/etc/services is owned by a system account and not writable by others (/etc/services는 시스템 계정 소유, 다른 사용자 쓰기 금지) — severity high, reads file metadata.

Checks that /etc/services is owned by root, bin or sys with mode 0644 or stricter. Not applicable when it does not exist (minimal images without netbase).

**Why.** Changing a service's port number in /etc/services can expose or hide it.

**Fix.** Run `chown root /etc/services` and `chmod 644 /etc/services`.

#### `files.setid-outside-system-dirs`

No set-ID programs outside the system program directories (시스템 디렉터리 밖의 SUID·SGID 파일 없음) — severity high, lists what violates it.

Lists files with the set-user-ID or set-group-ID bit outside /usr/bin, /usr/sbin, /usr/lib, /usr/lib64, /usr/libexec, /bin, /sbin, /lib and /lib64, such as in home directories, /tmp, /var, /opt or /srv.

**Why.** Distributions install their set-ID programs in the system directories; one anywhere else is usually a leftover or a backdoor that grants its owner's rights to whoever runs it.

**Fix.** Remove the set-ID bits (`chmod u-s,g-s`) or the file, unless the software needs them.

#### `files.shadow-perms`

/etc/shadow is owned by root and readable by root only (/etc/shadow는 root 소유, root만 읽기) — severity high, reads file metadata.

Checks that /etc/shadow is owned by root with mode 0400 or stricter. Debian-family systems ship it as 0640 with group shadow, which this check reports.

**Why.** Password hashes in /etc/shadow can be cracked offline by anyone who can read them.

**Fix.** Run `chown root /etc/shadow` and `chmod 400 /etc/shadow`.

#### `files.startup-scripts`

Start-up scripts and units are owned by root and not writable by others (시작 스크립트와 유닛은 root 소유, 다른 사용자 쓰기 금지) — severity high, reads file metadata.

Checks that SysV init scripts, rc.local and the systemd units (services, timers, sockets, paths and their drop-in files) in /etc/systemd/system, and the services in /usr/lib/systemd/system, are owned by root and writable by no one else (mode 0755 or stricter).

**Why.** These run as root at boot; whoever can change one gets root at the next restart.

**Fix.** Run `chown root` and `chmod go-w` on each listed file.

#### `files.sudoers-perms`

sudoers files are owned by root and not writable by others (sudoers 파일은 root 소유, 다른 사용자 쓰기 금지) — severity medium, reads file metadata.

Checks that /etc/sudoers and the files in /etc/sudoers.d are owned by root with mode 0640 or stricter.

**Why.** Whoever can change the sudo rules can give themselves root.

**Fix.** Run `chown root` and `chmod 440` on each file (visudo keeps them that way).

#### `files.suspicious-hidden-names`

No files or directories named only of dots and spaces (점과 공백만으로 된 이름의 파일·디렉터리 없음) — severity low, lists what violates it.

Lists files and directories on local filesystems whose name is made only of dots and spaces (other than "." and ".."), such as "..." or ". ". Nothing legitimate needs such a name, and it hides a directory among the entries of a listing.

**Why.** A directory named "..." or ". " is easy to overlook next to "." and "..", which makes it a place to hide files.

**Fix.** Look at what the entry holds, then remove or rename it.

#### `files.syslog-conf-perms`

syslog configuration is owned by a system account and not readable by others (syslog 설정은 시스템 계정 소유, 다른 사용자 읽기 금지) — severity high, reads file metadata.

Checks that /etc/syslog.conf, /etc/rsyslog.conf and /etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf are owned by root, bin or sys with mode 0640 or stricter. Not applicable without a syslog daemon configuration.

**Why.** Whoever can change the logging configuration can hide their tracks.

**Fix.** Run `chown root` and `chmod 640` on each file.

#### `files.unowned`

No files without an owner (소유자·그룹이 없는 파일 없음) — severity high, lists what violates it.

Lists files and directories on local filesystems whose owner or group has no account in /etc/passwd or /etc/group.

**Why.** A file left behind by a deleted account belongs to whoever is next given its UID or GID.

**Fix.** Give each listed file an owner and group (`chown`), or remove it.

#### `files.world-writable`

No world-writable files, and no world-writable directories without the sticky bit (모든 사용자 쓰기 가능 파일·디렉터리 없음) — severity high, lists what violates it.

Lists regular files that every user can write, and directories every user can write that lack the sticky bit (so anyone can delete or replace others' files there), on local filesystems.

**Why.** Anyone can change a world-writable file; if a privileged program or user reads or runs it, that becomes a way to gain their rights.

**Fix.** Remove write permission for others (`chmod o-w`), or set the sticky bit on shared directories (`chmod +t`).

#### `homes.exists`

Accounts that can log in have a home directory (로그인 가능 계정의 홈 디렉터리 존재) — severity medium, lists what violates it.

Lists accounts with a login shell whose home directory does not exist.

**Why.** Without a home directory a user logs in to "/", and startup files and keys end up in unexpected places.

**Fix.** Create the home directory (`mkhomedir_helper <user>`), or remove or lock the account.

#### `homes.owner-perms`

Home directories belong to their accounts and others cannot write them (홈 디렉터리는 계정 본인 소유, 다른 사용자 쓰기 금지) — severity medium, lists what violates it.

Lists accounts with a login shell whose home directory is owned by another account or is writable by others.

**Why.** Whoever can write a home directory can replace its startup files and keys.

**Fix.** Run `chown <user> <home>` and `chmod o-w <home>` for each listed account.

#### `homes.startup-files`

Users' startup files belong to them and others cannot change them (사용자 시작 파일은 본인·root 소유, 다른 사용자 쓰기 금지) — severity high, lists what violates it.

Lists accounts whose shell startup files (.profile, .bashrc, .bash_profile, ...) are owned by someone other than the account or root, are writable by group or others, or are symbolic links to missing files.

**Why.** A startup file runs whenever its user logs in; whoever can change it runs commands as that user.

**Fix.** Run `chown <user>` and `chmod go-w` on each listed file, and remove links to missing files.

#### `services.bind-restrict-transfer`

BIND zone transfers are restricted (BIND 존 전송이 제한됨) — severity high, lists what violates it.

Lists the primary and secondary zones of /etc/named.conf (or /etc/bind/named.conf) and the files it includes that any host may transfer: no allow-transfer applies to the zone (BIND then allows everyone), or it contains any. allow-transfer is read from the zone, its view and options, and acl names are followed. The zones every installation defines for the host itself (localhost and the loopback reverse zones) are left out. Applies when BIND is started and has a configuration; another DNS server is services.review-dns-other.

**Why.** A zone transfer hands over every name in the zone, which maps the network for an attacker.

**Fix.** Set `allow-transfer { none; };` in options and list your secondaries (or a TSIG key) in the zones that need it.

#### `services.bind-restrict-update`

BIND dynamic updates are restricted (BIND 동적 업데이트가 제한됨) — severity high, lists what violates it.

Lists the primary zones of /etc/named.conf (or /etc/bind/named.conf) and the files it includes whose allow-update contains any. Dynamic updates are off unless allow-update or update-policy is set; addresses, keys and an update-policy count as restricted. Applies when BIND is started and has a configuration; another DNS server is services.review-dns-other.

**Why.** Whoever can update a zone can point its names at their own hosts.

**Fix.** Allow updates only with a key (`allow-update { key dhcp-updates; };`) or an update-policy, or remove allow-update.

#### `services.ftp-account-shell`

The ftp account cannot log in (ftp 계정 로그인 셸 제한) — severity medium, lists what violates it.

Checks that the ftp account, if it exists, has a shell such as /sbin/nologin or /bin/false.

**Why.** The ftp account exists for anonymous FTP; with a login shell it can become a way in.

**Fix.** Run `usermod -s /sbin/nologin ftp`.

#### `services.nfs-exports-restricted`

NFS exports are limited to the hosts that need them (NFS 공유가 필요한 호스트로 제한됨) — severity high, lists what violates it.

Lists the entries of /etc/exports and /etc/exports.d/*.exports that are open to every host (a client of "*", or only options, as in `/srv (rw)`, which is the usual slip of a space before the parenthesis) and the ones that let a remote root act as root (no_root_squash). An export added at run time with exportfs is not in these files. Applies when an NFS server is started and /etc/exports or /etc/exports.d is there; otherwise services.review-nfs-other asks for a review.

**Why.** An export open to everyone, or without root_squash, hands the shared files to any host on the network.

**Fix.** List the hosts or networks that need each export (`/srv/data 192.0.2.0/24(rw)`), put no space before the parenthesis, and keep root_squash.

#### `services.no-automount`

The automounter is not started (automountd 미사용) — severity high, lists what violates it.

Lists the ways the automounter (autofs) is started: enabled units, units running now, init scripts and inetd/xinetd entries, found by service name or program.

**Why.** The automounter mounts file systems on access, which can expose local or remote file systems unexpectedly.

**Fix.** Disable autofs (`systemctl disable --now autofs`) if nothing needs it.

#### `services.no-dos-prone`

Services that amplify traffic are not started (DoS 공격에 취약한 서비스 미사용) — severity high, lists what violates it.

Lists the ways the echo, discard, daytime and chargen services are started: enabled units, units running now, init scripts and inetd/xinetd entries, found by service name.

**Why.** These test services answer anyone, so attackers can bounce and amplify traffic through them.

**Fix.** Disable them in inetd/xinetd (`disable = yes`).

#### `services.no-finger`

The finger service is not started (finger 서비스 미사용) — severity high, lists what violates it.

Lists the ways the finger service (fingerd, cfingerd) is started: enabled units, units running now, init scripts and inetd/xinetd entries, found by service name or program.

**Why.** finger tells anyone on the network who your users are and when they log in.

**Fix.** Disable the service: remove its inetd/xinetd entry, or `systemctl disable --now` its unit.

#### `services.no-nfs-server`

The NFS server is not started (NFS 서버 미사용) — severity high, lists what violates it.

Lists the ways the NFS server is started: enabled units, units running now, init scripts and inetd/xinetd entries, found by service name or program.

**Why.** An NFS server shares files over the network; when nobody needs it, it is only exposure.

**Fix.** Disable it (`systemctl disable --now nfs-server`) if no client needs these shares.

#### `services.no-nis`

NIS is not used (NIS 서비스 미사용) — severity high, lists what violates it.

Lists the ways the NIS server and client daemons (ypserv, ypbind, yppasswdd, ypxfrd) are started: enabled units, units running now, init scripts and inetd/xinetd entries, found by service name or program.

**Why.** NIS hands out account data, including password hashes, with weak protection.

**Fix.** Disable the NIS daemons and use a directory service with encryption, such as LDAP over TLS.

#### `services.no-r-services`

The r-services are not started (r 계열 서비스 미사용) — severity high, lists what violates it.

Lists the ways rsh, rlogin and rexec (inetd's shell, login and exec services, or their units) are started: enabled units, units running now, init scripts and inetd/xinetd entries, found by service name or program.

**Why.** The r-services send passwords in clear text and trust hosts by address.

**Fix.** Disable rsh, rlogin and rexec and use SSH instead.

#### `services.no-rpc`

Legacy RPC services are not started (불필요한 RPC 서비스 미사용) — severity high, lists what violates it.

Lists the ways legacy RPC services (rusersd, rwalld, sprayd, rstatd, rexd, the CDE calendar and tooltalk daemons, sadmind, pcnfsd, ypupdated, rquotad, nisd) are started: enabled units, units running now, init scripts and inetd/xinetd entries, found by service name or program.

**Why.** These RPC services have a long record of remote exploits and are rarely needed. rpc.statd is not listed: NFS clients use it for file locking (services.no-nfs-server covers NFS servers).

**Fix.** Disable each listed service.

#### `services.no-snmp`

SNMP is not started unless needed (SNMP 서비스 미사용) — severity medium, lists what violates it.

Lists the ways the SNMP agent (snmpd) is started: enabled units, units running now, init scripts and inetd/xinetd entries, found by service name or program.

**Why.** An SNMP agent exposes system details and, misconfigured, lets others change settings.

**Fix.** Disable snmpd if nothing monitors this host through SNMP; otherwise waive this check and secure snmpd.

#### `services.no-telnet`

Telnet is not started (텔넷 서비스 미사용) — severity medium, lists what violates it.

Lists the ways the telnet service is started: enabled units, units running now, init scripts and inetd/xinetd entries, found by service name or program.

**Why.** Telnet sends passwords and sessions in clear text.

**Fix.** Disable telnet and use SSH.

#### `services.no-tftp-talk`

tftp and talk are not started (tftp, talk 서비스 미사용) — severity high, lists what violates it.

Lists the ways the tftp, talk and ntalk services are started: enabled units, units running now, init scripts and inetd/xinetd entries, found by service name or program.

**Why.** tftp serves files without authentication; talk is an old, unneeded chat service.

**Fix.** Disable them.

#### `services.postfix-no-open-relay`

Postfix does not relay for everyone (Postfix가 모든 곳의 메일을 중계하지 않음) — severity high, lists what violates it.

Reads /etc/postfix/main.cf for the two ways to make Postfix an open relay: mynetworks with an entry that matches every address (a prefix length of 0), and a relay list (smtpd_relay_restrictions) that reaches a bare permit, or its end (which permits), without a reject_unauth_destination, defer_unauth_destination or bare reject or defer first, unless the recipient list refuses. The defaults of Postfix 2.10 and later are safe, so only what main.cf sets can fail this check. Not followed: lookup tables (hash: and cidr: entries), policy services and mynetworks_style. A master.cf option that overrides one of these parameters makes the result ERROR, since it cannot be judged from main.cf. Applies when Postfix is started and has a main.cf; another mail server is services.review-mail-relay-other.

**Why.** An open relay sends spam for anyone and gets the server blocked.

**Fix.** Set `mynetworks` to your own networks and end the relay restrictions with `defer_unauth_destination` (or `reject_unauth_destination`), with no bare `permit` before it, and do not let a list end without it.

#### `services.postfix-no-vrfy`

Postfix does not answer VRFY (Postfix가 VRFY 명령에 응답하지 않음) — severity medium, compares one setting.

Checks disable_vrfy_command in /etc/postfix/main.cf. Postfix answers VRFY, which tells whether an address exists, unless it is set to yes (or on, true, 1). A master.cf option that overrides it makes the result ERROR. Applies when Postfix is started and has a main.cf; another mail server is services.review-mail-relay-other.

**Why.** VRFY lets anyone test which accounts exist on the server.

**Fix.** Set `disable_vrfy_command = yes` in /etc/postfix/main.cf and reload Postfix.

#### `services.review-anonymous-sharing`

Review anonymous access to file-sharing services (파일 공유 서비스 익명 접근 검토) — severity high, a review (`MANUAL`).

Applies when a file-sharing service the other checks do not read is started: NFS, an FTP server other than vsftpd, vsftpd or Samba without their configuration file (vsftpd with a vsftpd.conf is services.vsftpd-no-anonymous, Samba with an smb.conf is services.samba-no-guest); then shows how, for a review of its configuration. Not applicable otherwise.

**Why.** Anonymous access to shared files lets anyone read, and sometimes write, them.

**Fix.** Check that the listed services allow no anonymous access: vsftpd `anonymous_enable=NO`, NFS exports limited to known hosts with root_squash, no Samba guest access.

#### `services.review-dns-other`

Review zone transfers and updates of the DNS server (DNS 서버의 존 전송·업데이트 설정 검토) — severity high, a review (`MANUAL`).

Applies when a DNS server other than BIND is started, or BIND is started and has no named.conf at the usual places (BIND with a configuration is checked by services.bind-restrict-transfer and services.bind-restrict-update); then shows how it was started, for a review of its configuration. Not applicable otherwise.

**Why.** Zone transfers map your network for attackers, and open dynamic updates let them change it.

**Fix.** Check that the DNS server allows zone transfers only to its secondaries and dynamic updates only with keys or not at all.

#### `services.review-dns-server`

Review the DNS server (DNS 서버 설정 검토) — severity high, a review (`MANUAL`).

Applies when a DNS server is started; then shows how, for a review of its configuration. Not applicable otherwise.

**Why.** Zone transfers map your network for attackers, and open dynamic updates let them change it.

**Fix.** Check that the DNS server is up to date, allows zone transfers only to its secondaries (BIND allow-transfer) and dynamic updates only with keys or not at all (allow-update, update-policy).

#### `services.review-ftp-other`

Review the FTP server's banner, encryption and root login (FTP 서버의 배너·암호화·root 로그인 설정 검토) — severity high, a review (`MANUAL`).

Applies when an FTP server other than vsftpd is started, or vsftpd is started and has no vsftpd.conf (vsftpd with a configuration is checked by services.vsftpd-banner, services.vsftpd-tls and services.vsftpd-no-root); then shows how it was started, for a review of its configuration. Not applicable otherwise.

**Why.** Plain FTP sends passwords in clear text, a version banner tells attackers which exploits to try, and a root login over FTP exposes the host.

**Fix.** Check that the FTP server requires TLS (or is replaced by SFTP), hides its version in the banner and refuses root (ftpusers).

#### `services.review-ftp-server`

Review the FTP server (FTP 서버 설정 검토) — severity medium, a review (`MANUAL`).

Applies when an FTP server is started; then shows how, for a review of its configuration. Not applicable otherwise.

**Why.** Plain FTP sends passwords in clear text, and a version banner tells attackers which exploits to try.

**Fix.** Check that the FTP server requires TLS (or is replaced by SFTP), hides its version in the banner, accepts connections only from the addresses that need it, and refuses root (ftpusers, user_list).

#### `services.review-mail-relay-other`

Review relaying and VRFY of the mail server (메일 서버의 중계·VRFY 설정 검토) — severity high, a review (`MANUAL`).

Applies when a mail server other than Postfix is started, or Postfix is started and has no /etc/postfix/main.cf (Postfix with a main.cf is checked by services.postfix-no-open-relay and services.postfix-no-vrfy); then shows how it was started, for a review of its configuration. Not applicable otherwise.

**Why.** An open mail server is used to send spam and to probe for accounts.

**Fix.** Check that the mail server relays only for your networks and authenticated users and rejects EXPN and VRFY (Sendmail: PrivacyOptions noexpn, novrfy).

#### `services.review-mail-server`

Review the mail server (메일 서버 설정 검토) — severity high, a review (`MANUAL`).

Applies when a mail server is started; then shows how, for a review of its configuration. Not applicable otherwise.

**Why.** An outdated or open mail server is used to send spam and to probe for accounts.

**Fix.** Check that the mail server is up to date, relays only for your networks and authenticated users, rejects EXPN and VRFY, and lets only the mail system run its queue (Sendmail: PrivacyOptions restrictqrun, noexpn, novrfy).

#### `services.review-network-access`

Review who can reach the services (서비스에 접근할 수 있는 대상 검토) — severity high, a review (`MANUAL`).

Lists what decides who can reach the host from the network: the host firewall services that are enabled (firewalld, ufw, nftables, iptables, netfilter-persistent) and, on a live host, the sockets listening on an address other than loopback.

**Why.** A service open to every address is exposed to everyone who can route to it.

**Fix.** Restrict each service that is not meant for everyone with a host firewall (nftables, iptables, firewalld, ufw) or the service's own access rules (TCP wrappers, allow lists), or bind it to the addresses that need it.

#### `services.review-nfs-other`

Review the NFS exports (NFS 공유 설정 검토) — severity high, a review (`MANUAL`).

Applies when an NFS server is started but /etc/exports and /etc/exports.d are not there (the exports may be made some other way, for example with exportfs at boot); then shows how it was started, for a review. With export files, services.nfs-exports-restricted decides. Not applicable otherwise.

**Why.** An export open to everyone, or without root_squash, hands the shared files to any host on the network.

**Fix.** Check the exports (`exportfs -v`): each is limited to the hosts that need it, never "*", and uses root_squash.

#### `services.review-remote-root-login`

Review root login through telnet and other remote terminal services (telnet 등 원격 터미널 서비스의 root 로그인 검토) — severity high, a review (`MANUAL`).

Applies when telnet or rlogin is started; then shows how, for a review of whether root can log in through it. Not applicable otherwise. The OpenSSH checks do not cover these services.

**Why.** A telnet or rlogin server lets root log in remotely unless its login stack refuses it, and it sends the password in clear text.

**Fix.** Turn the service off (services.no-telnet, services.no-r-services) and use SSH. If it must run, keep root out of it: on systems that still ship pam_securetty (older distributions), put `auth required pam_securetty.so` in its PAM login stack and remove every pts/N line from /etc/securetty; elsewhere, the service must refuse root by other means.

#### `services.review-snmp-agent`

Review the SNMP agent (SNMP 에이전트 설정 검토) — severity high, a review (`MANUAL`).

Applies when an SNMP agent is started but /etc/snmp/snmpd.conf is not there (it may take its configuration from elsewhere); then shows how it was started, for a review of its configuration. When the file is there, services.snmp-v3-only, services.snmp-community-strong and services.snmp-access-restricted decide. Not applicable otherwise.

**Why.** SNMP v1/v2c communities travel in clear text and default ones are the first thing scanners try.

**Fix.** Check that the SNMP agent accepts only SNMPv3 with authentication and privacy, uses no default or guessable community, and answers only the management hosts that need it.

#### `services.review-time-sync`

Review the time servers (시각 동기화 서버 검토) — severity low, a review (`MANUAL`).

Shows the time synchronization services that are started, to check their servers against your standard.

**Why.** A synchronized clock is only as good as the servers it follows.

**Fix.** Point the service at the time servers your organization approves (`server` or `pool` lines).

#### `services.samba-no-guest`

No Samba share is open to guests (게스트에게 열린 Samba 공유 없음) — severity high, lists what violates it.

Lists the shares of /etc/samba/smb.conf with "guest ok = yes" or "public = yes", on the share or as the default in [global]. The printer sections are not shares. An include or config file line is not followed and makes the result ERROR, as does another .conf next to smb.conf (smbd may be started with it). Applies when Samba is started and has an smb.conf; otherwise services.review-anonymous-sharing asks for a review.

**Why.** A share open to guests lets anyone who can reach the server read, and sometimes write, its files.

**Fix.** Set `guest ok = no` on the share (and remove `public = yes`), and give the users that need it Samba accounts.

#### `services.snmp-access-restricted`

SNMP answers only the hosts that need it (SNMP는 필요한 호스트에만 응답) — severity high, lists what violates it.

Lists the community entries of /etc/snmp/snmpd.conf and the files it includes that answer every source address while the agent is not limited to the host itself with agentAddress. On a live host, a UDP socket on port 161 that is open to other hosts also counts as not limited, since a listen address on the command line (for example in /etc/default/snmpd) overrides agentAddress. Applies when the agent is started and the configuration is at its usual place.

**Why.** An agent that answers any address with a community string can be asked by anyone who can reach it.

**Fix.** Give each community the management network as its source (`rocommunity name 10.0.0.0/8`), or set `agentAddress udp:127.0.0.1:161` if only the host itself needs it.

#### `services.snmp-community-strong`

SNMP community strings are not guessable (SNMP community 문자열은 추측하기 어려움) — severity high, lists what violates it.

Lists the community strings of /etc/snmp/snmpd.conf and the files it includes that are a well-known name (public, private, ...) or shorter than 8 characters. The strings themselves are never read into the result. Applies when the agent is started and the configuration is at its usual place.

**Why.** Default community names are the first thing scanners try; a short one falls to guessing.

**Fix.** Choose a community of at least 8 random characters, or move to SNMPv3 (services.snmp-v3-only).

#### `services.snmp-v3-only`

The SNMP agent has no SNMPv1 or v2c access (SNMP 에이전트에 SNMPv1·v2c 접근이 없음) — severity high, lists what violates it.

Lists the SNMPv1 and v2c access entries (rocommunity, rwcommunity, authcommunity, com2sec) of /etc/snmp/snmpd.conf and the files it includes. v1 and v2c send their community string in clear text and cannot authenticate a user. The security level of SNMPv3 users (rouser, rwuser) is not judged. Applies when the agent is started and its configuration is at the usual place; otherwise services.review-snmp-agent asks for a review.

**Why.** Whoever sniffs a community string can read, and with rwcommunity change, what the agent exposes.

**Fix.** Remove the community lines, create SNMPv3 users (`net-snmp-create-v3-user`) and give them rouser or rwuser lines with `authPriv`.

#### `services.time-sync`

A time synchronization service is started (시각 동기화 서비스 사용) — severity medium, evaluates an expression.

Checks that chrony, ntpd, ntpsec or systemd-timesyncd is enabled (as a unit or an init script), or running on a live host. Which servers it uses is for services.review-time-sync.

**Why.** Logs from hosts with drifting clocks cannot be correlated, and time-based protocols fail.

**Fix.** Enable a time synchronization service (`systemctl enable --now chronyd`).

#### `services.vsftpd-banner`

The vsftpd banner does not show the version (vsftpd 접속 배너에 버전이 없음) — severity low, evaluates an expression.

Checks what vsftpd tells a client that connects. Without ftpd_banner or banner_file it says "(vsFTPd x.y.z)"; a custom text or file that still contains a version number or the name vsftpd fails too. Only the default vsftpd.conf is read (a second default file or another .conf next to it makes the result ERROR). Applies when vsftpd is started and has a vsftpd.conf; another FTP server is services.review-ftp-other.

**Why.** A version banner tells attackers which exploits to try.

**Fix.** Set `ftpd_banner=Authorized users only.` in vsftpd.conf, with no version number and not the name vsftpd.

#### `services.vsftpd-no-anonymous`

vsftpd allows no anonymous login (vsftpd가 익명 로그인을 허용하지 않음) — severity high, compares one setting.

Checks anonymous_enable in vsftpd.conf. vsftpd allows anonymous logins unless it is set to NO (the packaged configurations set it). Only the default vsftpd.conf is read (a second default file or another .conf next to it makes the result ERROR). Applies when vsftpd is started and has a vsftpd.conf; otherwise services.review-anonymous-sharing asks for a review.

**Why.** Anonymous FTP lets anyone read, and sometimes write, the files it shares.

**Fix.** Set `anonymous_enable=NO` in vsftpd.conf and reload vsftpd.

#### `services.vsftpd-no-root`

root cannot log in to vsftpd (root가 vsftpd에 로그인할 수 없음) — severity medium, evaluates an expression.

Checks that root is refused: the FTP service's PAM stack has a pam_listfile line (item=user, sense=deny) whose file lists root (/etc/ftpusers, /etc/vsftpd/ftpusers), or userlist_enable makes vsftpd refuse root (a user list that holds it with userlist_deny=YES, or one that does not with userlist_deny=NO). Nested PAM includes are not followed, and a PAM rule before pam_listfile that may let root skip it (sufficient, an include) makes the result ERROR. Only the default vsftpd.conf is read (a second default file or another .conf next to it makes the result ERROR). Applies when vsftpd is started and has a vsftpd.conf; another FTP server is services.review-ftp-other.

**Why.** A root password sent over FTP, even over TLS, puts the whole host at the mercy of one login.

**Fix.** List root in /etc/ftpusers (or /etc/vsftpd/ftpusers) and keep the pam_listfile line in the vsftpd PAM service.

#### `services.vsftpd-tls`

vsftpd requires TLS (vsftpd가 TLS를 사용함) — severity medium, evaluates an expression.

Checks ssl_enable in vsftpd.conf and that local logins are still required to use it (force_local_logins_ssl, YES by default). Plain FTP sends passwords and files in clear text. Only the default vsftpd.conf is read (a second default file or another .conf next to it makes the result ERROR). Applies when vsftpd is started and has a vsftpd.conf; another FTP server is services.review-ftp-other.

**Why.** Plain FTP sends passwords in clear text.

**Fix.** Set `ssl_enable=YES` with a certificate (`rsa_cert_file`) in vsftpd.conf, or replace FTP by SFTP.

#### `ssh.match-permit-root-login`

No SSH Match block allows root login (SSH Match 블록의 root 로그인 허용 금지) — severity high, lists what violates it.

Lists Match blocks of the OpenSSH server configuration that set PermitRootLogin to anything but "no", which re-enables root login for the connections they match.

**Why.** A Match block overrides the global setting for matching connections, so a hardened global value can be undone for a whole network or user group.

**Fix.** Remove PermitRootLogin from the Match block or set it to "no" there as well.

#### `ssh.permit-root-login`

SSH does not allow direct root login (SSH root 직접 로그인 차단) — severity high, compares one setting.

Checks the global PermitRootLogin setting of the OpenSSH server. On a live host the effective value comes from `sshd -T`, so the default of the installed version counts.

**Why.** Direct root logins remove accountability and expose the most privileged account to password guessing and stolen keys.

**Fix.** Set `PermitRootLogin no` in /etc/ssh/sshd_config (or a file it includes) and reload sshd. Administrators log in with their own accounts and use sudo or su.
